source.text: וַיְהִ֣י׀בְּחֹ֣דֶשׁ נִיסָ֗ן שְׁנַ֥ת עֶשְׂרִ֛ים לְאַרְתַּחְשַׁ֥סְתְּא הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ יַ֣יִן לְפָנָ֑יו וָאֶשָּׂ֤א אֶת־הַיַּ֨יִן֙ וָאֶתְּנָ֣ה לַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וְלֹא־הָיִ֥יתִי רַ֖ע לְפָנָֽיו׃

records.literal_gloss: And it was in [the] month [of] Nisan, [in the] year twenty of Artaxerxes the king, wine [was] before him, and I took up the wine and gave [it] to the king; and not I had been sad before him.

en.L: And it came about in the month of Nisan, in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes the king, that wine was before him, and I took up the wine and gave it to the king. And I had not been sad before him.
en.B: In the month of Nisan, in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes, when wine was set before him, I picked up the wine and gave it to the king. I had never been sad in his presence before.
en.R: Four months later, in the month of Nisan, in the twentieth year that Artaxerxes was king, wine was brought to the king during a meal. I picked up the wine and handed it to him. Until then I had never looked sad when I was with him.

decisions.choice: Nisan in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes: the first month, about March-April, 445 BC
decisions.reason: Nisan is the Babylonian name of the first month of the year, in spring (Esther 3:7). It is four months after Kislev (1:1). The king is Artaxerxes I, who ruled Persia from 465 to 424 BC, the king who had also sent Ezra (Ezra 7:1, 7).

decisions.choice: I had not been sad before him: he had never before looked sad in the king's presence
decisions.reason: The clause explains why the king noticed (verse 2). A servant was expected to look cheerful before the king; a sad face could be read as discontent (compare Esther 4:2, where no one in mourning clothes could enter the king's gate).

decisions.choice: Four months later; during a meal
decisions.reason: Readable states the time since Kislev (1:1) and that the wine was served at the king's table, which the setting implies.

source.text: וַיֹּאמֶר֩ לִ֨י הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ מַדּ֣וּעַ׀פָּנֶ֣יךָ רָעִ֗ים וְאַתָּה֙ אֵֽינְךָ֣ חוֹלֶ֔ה אֵ֣ין זֶ֔ה כִּי־אִ֖ם רֹ֣עַֽ לֵ֑ב וָאִירָ֖א הַרְבֵּ֥ה מְאֹֽד׃

records.literal_gloss: And said to me the king, why [is] your face sad, and you not [are] sick? Not [is] this [anything] except sadness of heart. And I was afraid very greatly.

en.L: And the king said to me, "Why is your face sad, when you are not sick? This is nothing but sadness of heart." And I was very greatly afraid.
en.B: So the king asked me, "Why do you look so sad? You are not sick. This can only be sadness of heart." Then I was terribly afraid.
en.R: The king asked me, "Why do you look so sad? You are not sick. Something must be troubling you deeply." I was very frightened.

decisions.choice: your face is bad, badness of heart: you look sad; this is grief within
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says the face is "bad" and the heart has "badness": here this means sadness and inner distress, not wickedness (compare Genesis 40:7; Proverbs 15:13).

decisions.choice: I was very greatly afraid: a sad face before the king was dangerous
decisions.reason: A Persian king could take a servant's gloom as a sign of discontent or disloyalty, and Nehemiah was about to ask him to change a policy he had himself put in place (Ezra 4:21). He had reason to fear.

decisions.choice: Something must be troubling you deeply
decisions.reason: Readable says in plain words what "sadness of heart" means.

source.text: וָאֹמַ֣ר לַמֶּ֔לֶךְ הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ לְעוֹלָ֣ם יִחְיֶ֑ה מַדּ֜וּעַ לֹא־יֵרְע֣וּ פָנַ֗י אֲשֶׁ֨ר הָעִ֜יר בֵּית־קִבְר֤וֹת אֲבֹתַי֙ חֲרֵבָ֔ה וּשְׁעָרֶ֖יהָ אֻכְּל֥וּ בָאֵֽשׁ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And I said to the king, the king forever may he live! Why not will be sad my face, when the city, [the] house of [the] graves of my fathers, [is] desolate and its gates have been consumed by fire?

en.L: And I said to the king, "May the king live forever! Why should my face not be sad, when the city, the place of my fathers' graves, lies desolate, and its gates have been consumed by fire?"
en.B: I said to the king, "May the king live forever! Why should I not look sad, when the city where my ancestors are buried lies in ruins and its gates have been destroyed by fire?"
en.R: I answered the king, "May Your Majesty live forever! How can I help looking sad? The city where my ancestors are buried is in ruins, and its gates have been burned down."

decisions.choice: may the king live forever: the respectful greeting to a king
decisions.reason: This was the usual way to address a king in the ancient Near East (1 Kings 1:31; Daniel 2:4; 6:22).

decisions.choice: the city, the house of my fathers' graves: Jerusalem, where his ancestors are buried
decisions.reason: Nehemiah does not name Jerusalem, but speaks of it as the place of his ancestors' graves (also verse 5). Honor for ancestors' tombs was something any king would understand. The wording may also avoid naming a city whose walls the king had stopped from being rebuilt (Ezra 4:21).

decisions.choice: ancestors
decisions.reason: "Fathers" here means forefathers, so Balanced and Readable say "ancestors". Literal keeps "fathers".

decisions.choice: Your Majesty
decisions.reason: Readable uses the English form of address to a king for the third-person "the king".

source.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר לִי֙ הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ עַל־מַה־זֶּ֖ה אַתָּ֣ה מְבַקֵּ֑שׁ וָֽאֶתְפַּלֵּ֔ל אֶל־אֱלֹהֵ֖י הַשָּׁמָֽיִם׃

records.literal_gloss: And said to me the king, for what [is] this [that] you [are] requesting? And I prayed to [the] God of the heavens.

en.L: And the king said to me, "What is it that you are requesting?" So I prayed to the God of heaven.
en.B: The king said to me, "What is it you want?" So I prayed to the God of heaven,
en.R: The king asked me, "What do you want?" I prayed silently to the God of heaven,

decisions.choice: I prayed to the God of heaven: a short, silent prayer before he answered
decisions.reason: Nehemiah speaks to the king at once in verse 5, so this prayer was a quick one in his heart. His long prayer of chapter 1 had already asked for this moment (1:11).

decisions.choice: prayed silently
decisions.reason: Readable says the prayer was silent, which the setting implies: he answers the king straight away. It is an inference.

source.text: וָאֹמַ֣ר לַמֶּ֔לֶךְ אִם־עַל־הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ ט֔וֹב וְאִם־יִיטַ֥ב עַבְדְּךָ֖ לְפָנֶ֑יךָ אֲשֶׁ֧ר תִּשְׁלָחֵ֣נִי אֶל־יְהוּדָ֗ה אֶל־עִ֛יר קִבְר֥וֹת אֲבֹתַ֖י וְאֶבְנֶֽנָּה׃

records.literal_gloss: And I said to the king, if to the king [it is] good, and if is pleasing your servant before you, that you send me to Judah, to [the] city of [the] graves of my fathers, and I will rebuild it.

en.L: and I said to the king, "If it is good to the king, and if your servant is pleasing before you, send me to Judah, to the city of my fathers' graves, so that I may rebuild it."
en.B: and I said to the king, "If it pleases the king, and if your servant has found favor with you, send me to Judah, to the city where my ancestors are buried, so that I can rebuild it."
en.R: Then I answered the king, "If it pleases Your Majesty, and if you are happy with me, your servant, please send me to Judah, to the city where my ancestors are buried. Let me rebuild it."

decisions.choice: if it is good to the king: if it pleases the king
decisions.reason: The polite formula for a request to a king (Esther 1:19; 5:4; 7:3).

decisions.choice: I will rebuild it: rebuild the city
decisions.reason: The request is to rebuild the city, which in practice meant first its walls and gates (2:8, 17). The pronoun refers to "the city".

decisions.choice: your servant
decisions.reason: Speaking of oneself as "your servant" is court language before a king. The project uses "servant" at every level for a king's official or for this courtesy.

source.text: וַיֹּאמֶר֩ לִ֨י הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ וְהַשֵּׁגַ֣ל׀יוֹשֶׁ֣בֶת אֶצְל֗וֹ עַד־מָתַ֛י יִהְיֶ֥ה מַֽהֲלָכֲךָ֖ וּמָתַ֣י תָּשׁ֑וּב וַיִּיטַ֤ב לִפְנֵֽי־הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ וַיִּשְׁלָחֵ֔נִי וָֽאֶתְּנָ֥ה ל֖וֹ זְמָֽן׃

records.literal_gloss: And said to me the king, and the queen [was] sitting beside him, until when will be your journey, and when will you return? And it was good before the king, and he sent me, and I gave to him a time.

en.L: And the king said to me, while the queen was sitting beside him, "How long will your journey be, and when will you return?" And it pleased the king to send me, and I gave him a time.
en.B: The king, with the queen sitting beside him, asked me, "How long will you be gone, and when will you come back?" So it pleased the king to send me, and I set a time for him.
en.R: The queen was sitting beside the king. He asked me, "How long will your trip take? When will you come back?" The king was pleased to send me, and I told him when I would return.

decisions.choice: the queen: the king's consort
decisions.reason: The word is a rare title for the king's wife or consort (Psalm 45:10). The text says no more of her; it only notes that she was there.

decisions.choice: I gave him a time: I set a date for my return
decisions.reason: Nehemiah fixed how long he would be away. He in fact governed Judah twelve years (5:14) and later returned to the king (13:6); the text does not say whether the first time set was that long or was later extended.

decisions.choice: it pleased the king to send me
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable join the two clauses "it was good before the king, and he sent me" into one, which is what they say together.

source.text: וָאוֹמַר֮ לַמֶּלֶךְ֒ אִם־עַל־הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ ט֔וֹב אִגְּרוֹת֙ יִתְּנוּ־לִ֔י עַֽל־פַּחֲו֖וֹת עֵ֣בֶר הַנָּהָ֑ר אֲשֶׁר֙ יַעֲבִיר֔וּנִי עַ֥ד אֲשֶׁר־אָב֖וֹא אֶל־יְהוּדָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And I said to the king, if to the king [it is] good, letters let them give to me to [the] governors of Beyond the River, that they let me pass through until I come to Judah,

en.L: And I said to the king, "If it is good to the king, let letters be given to me for the governors of Beyond the River, so that they may let me pass through until I come to Judah,
en.B: I also said to the king, "If it pleases the king, let me be given letters to the governors of the province Beyond the River, so that they will let me pass through until I reach Judah,
en.R: I also said to the king, "If it pleases Your Majesty, please give me letters to the governors of the province west of the Euphrates River. Then they will let me travel safely through their lands until I reach Judah.

decisions.choice: the governors of Beyond the River: the Persian officials of the lands west of the Euphrates
decisions.reason: "Beyond the River" was the Persian name for the province west of the Euphrates, seen from the empire's center: Syria, Phoenicia, Samaria and Judah (Ezra 4:10; 8:36). Its governors ruled the districts Nehemiah would pass through.

decisions.choice: letters that let me pass through: written orders of safe conduct
decisions.reason: Letters from the king were his authority: they told the officials to let the bearer travel and to help him (compare Ezra 7:21; 8:36).

decisions.choice: the province Beyond the River (Balanced); the province west of the Euphrates River (Readable)
decisions.reason: The project's wording for this name: Literal keeps the bare name, Balanced adds that it is a province, Readable says where it was.

source.text: וְאִגֶּ֡רֶת אֶל־אָסָף֩ שֹׁמֵ֨ר הַפַּרְדֵּ֜ס אֲשֶׁ֣ר לַמֶּ֗לֶךְ אֲשֶׁ֣ר יִתֶּן־לִ֣י עֵצִ֡ים לְ֠קָרוֹת אֶת־שַׁעֲרֵ֨י הַבִּירָ֤ה אֲשֶׁר־לַבַּ֨יִת֙ וּלְחוֹמַ֣ת הָעִ֔יר וְלַבַּ֖יִת אֲשֶׁר־אָב֣וֹא אֵלָ֑יו וַיִּתֶּן־לִ֣י הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ כְּיַד־אֱלֹהַ֖י הַטּוֹבָ֥ה עָלָֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: and a letter to Asaph, keeper of the forest which [is] to the king, that he give to me timber to make beams [for] the gates of the citadel which [is] to the house, and for [the] wall of the city, and for the house which I will go into. And gave to me the king according to the hand of my God, the good, on me.

en.L: and a letter to Asaph, keeper of the king's forest, that he may give me timber to make beams for the gates of the citadel which belongs to the house, and for the wall of the city, and for the house that I will enter." And the king gave them to me, according to the good hand of my God upon me.
en.B: and a letter to Asaph, keeper of the king's forest, so that he will give me timber to make beams for the gates of the fortress by the temple, for the city wall, and for the house I will live in." And the king granted me these things, because the good hand of my God was on me.
en.R: And please give me a letter to Asaph, who is in charge of the king's forest. Then he will give me wood to make beams for the gates of the fortress next to the temple, for the city wall, and for the house where I will live." The king gave me what I asked for, because my God was kindly helping me.

decisions.choice: Asaph, keeper of the king's forest: the official over a royal woodland
decisions.reason: The word for "forest" is a Persian loanword for an enclosed park or woodland (Song of Songs 4:13; Ecclesiastes 2:5); through Greek the same word later came to mean paradise. The text does not say where this forest was.

decisions.choice: the citadel which belongs to the house: the fortress beside the temple
decisions.reason: "The house" here is the temple, the house of God. The citadel was a fortress guarding it, probably on its north side (7:2 names its commander); a later fortress there was called Antonia.

decisions.choice: the house that I will enter: the house where Nehemiah would live
decisions.reason: Most likely Nehemiah's own residence as the king's representative. The temple was already standing (Ezra 6:15), so this is not a request to rebuild it.

decisions.choice: according to the good hand of my God upon me: because God was kindly at work for me
decisions.reason: God's "hand" on someone is his power at work for them. Ezra uses the same phrase of the king granting his requests (Ezra 7:6, 9, 28; 8:18). Nehemiah gives the credit to God, not to his own skill.

decisions.choice: the fortress by the temple
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "temple" for "the house", which is what it means here, and "fortress" for the citadel.

source.text: וָֽאָב֗וֹא אֶֽל־פַּֽחֲווֹת֙עֵ֣בֶר הַנָּהָ֔ר וָאֶתְּנָ֣ה לָהֶ֔ם אֵ֖ת אִגְּר֣וֹת הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וַיִּשְׁלַ֤ח עִמִּי֙ הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ שָׂ֥רֵי חַ֖יִל וּפָרָשִֽׁים׃פ

records.literal_gloss: And I came to [the] governors of Beyond the River and gave to them the letters of the king. And had sent with me the king commanders of [the] army and horsemen.

en.L: And I came to the governors of Beyond the River and gave them the king's letters. And the king had sent with me commanders of the army and horsemen.
en.B: So I came to the governors of the province Beyond the River and gave them the king's letters. The king had also sent army commanders and horsemen with me.
en.R: So I went to the governors of the province west of the Euphrates River and gave them the king's letters. The king had also sent army commanders and soldiers on horses to go with me.

decisions.choice: the king had sent officers of the army and horsemen: a military escort
decisions.reason: An armed escort protected Nehemiah on the road and showed the king's authority. Ezra, thirteen years earlier, had been ashamed to ask the king for one, having said that God's hand protects those who seek him (Ezra 8:22). The text states both without judging either.

decisions.choice: commanders
decisions.reason: The project's wording for this word of rank in a military setting is "commanders" at every level.

source.text: וַיִּשְׁמַ֞ע סַנְבַלַּ֣ט הַחֹרֹנִ֗י וְטֽוֹבִיָּה֙ הָעֶ֣בֶד הָֽעַמֹּנִ֔י וַיֵּ֥רַע לָהֶ֖ם רָעָ֣ה גְדֹלָ֑ה אֲשֶׁר־בָּ֥א אָדָ֔ם לְבַקֵּ֥שׁ טוֹבָ֖ה לִבְנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: And heard Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite, and it was bad to them, a bad [thing], great, that had come a man to seek good for [the] sons of Israel.

en.L: And when Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite, heard, it was very bad in their eyes that a man had come to seek the good of the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel.
en.B: When Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite official heard of it, they were greatly displeased that someone had come to seek the welfare of the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}}.
en.R: Sanballat from Horon and Tobiah, the Ammonite official, heard about this. They were very upset that someone had come to help the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}}.

decisions.choice: Sanballat the Horonite: the governor of Samaria
decisions.reason: A letter found at Elephantine in Egypt, written in 407 BC, names Sanballat as governor of Samaria, the province north of Judah. "Horonite" probably means he came from Beth-horon, northwest of Jerusalem (Joshua 16:3), though Horonaim in Moab is also possible.

decisions.choice: Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite: an official, of Ammonite descent or over Ammonite land
decisions.reason: "Servant" here is the title of an official serving the king, as on seals of the period. Tobiah was linked to Ammon, east of the Jordan, and had family ties with leading people in Jerusalem (6:17-18; 13:4).

decisions.choice: it was bad to them, a great bad thing: they were very displeased
decisions.reason: The doubled "bad" is strong: they were deeply displeased. "The good of the Israelites" in the same verse is its opposite: their welfare.

decisions.choice: official
decisions.reason: The project renders "servant" as the title of a king's official with "official" at Balanced and Readable; Literal keeps "servant".

source.text: וָאָב֖וֹא אֶל־יְרוּשָׁלִָ֑ם וָאֱהִי־שָׁ֖ם יָמִ֥ים שְׁלֹשָֽׁה׃

records.literal_gloss: And I came to Jerusalem, and I was there days, three.

en.L: And I came to Jerusalem and was there three days.
en.B: So I came to Jerusalem, and I was there three days.
en.R: I arrived in Jerusalem and rested there for three days.

decisions.choice: three days: a time of rest after the journey
decisions.reason: Ezra's company also rested three days after arriving (Ezra 8:32). The journey from Susa took months (Ezra 7:9). Only after this pause does Nehemiah act (verse 12).

decisions.choice: rested there
decisions.reason: Readable says what the three days were for, which the parallel with Ezra 8:32 suggests.

source.text: וָאָק֣וּם׀לַ֗יְלָה אֲנִי֮ וַאֲנָשִׁ֣ים׀מְעַט֮ עִמִּי֒ וְלֹא־הִגַּ֣דְתִּי לְאָדָ֔ם מָ֗ה אֱלֹהַי֙ נֹתֵ֣ן אֶל־לִבִּ֔י לַעֲשׂ֖וֹת לִירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם וּבְהֵמָה֙ אֵ֣ין עִמִּ֔י כִּ֚י אִם־הַבְּהֵמָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר אֲנִ֖י רֹכֵ֥ב בָּֽהּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And I arose [by] night, I and men, a few, with me, and not I had told to anyone what my God [was] putting into my heart to do for Jerusalem; and an animal not [was] with me except the animal which I [was] riding on it.

en.L: And I arose in the night, I and a few men with me. And I had not told anyone what my God was putting into my heart to do for Jerusalem. And there was no animal with me except the animal I was riding.
en.B: Then I got up during the night, I and a few men with me. I had not told anyone what my God was putting into my heart to do for Jerusalem. There was no animal with me except the one I was riding.
en.R: Then I got up in the middle of the night and went out with a few men. I had not told anyone what my God had moved me to do for Jerusalem. The only animal with us was the one I was riding.

decisions.choice: what my God was putting into my heart: what God was moving me to do
decisions.reason: To put something in someone's heart is to give them the desire and resolve to do it (Ezra 7:27; Nehemiah 7:5). Nehemiah sees the plan as God's.

decisions.choice: by night, few men, telling no one, one animal: a secret inspection
decisions.reason: Nehemiah kept his plan to himself until he had seen the walls, so that no one, friend or enemy (verses 10, 16), could act on it first. A single animal made less noise than a group of riders.

decisions.choice: had moved me to do
decisions.reason: Readable says in plain words what "putting into my heart" means.

source.text: וָאֵצְאָ֨ה בְשַֽׁעַר־הַגַּ֜יא לַ֗יְלָה וְאֶל־פְּנֵי֙ עֵ֣ין הַתַּנִּ֔ין וְאֶל־שַׁ֖עַר הָאַשְׁפֹּ֑ת וָאֱהִ֨י שֹׂבֵ֜ר בְּחוֹמֹ֤ת יְרוּשָׁלִַ֨ם֙ אֲשֶׁר־הֵ֣ם׀פְּרוּצִ֔ים וּשְׁעָרֶ֖יהָ אֻכְּל֥וּ בָאֵֽשׁ׃

records.literal_gloss: And I went out by [the] gate of the valley [by] night, and toward [the] face of [the] Spring of the Dragon and to [the] gate of the dung, and I was examining the walls of Jerusalem which they [were] broken down, and its gates had been consumed by fire.

en.L: And I went out by night through the Valley Gate, toward the Dragon Spring and to the Dung Gate, and I was examining the walls of Jerusalem, which were broken down, and its gates, which had been consumed by fire.
en.B: I went out by night through the Valley Gate toward the Dragon Spring and the Dung Gate. I inspected the walls of Jerusalem, which had been broken down, and its gates, which had been destroyed by fire.
en.R: That night I went out through the Valley Gate and rode past the Dragon Spring to the Dung Gate. I looked carefully at the walls of Jerusalem, which had been broken down, and at its gates, which had been burned.

decisions.choice: the Valley Gate, the Dragon Spring, the Dung Gate: places on the west and south of the city
decisions.reason: The Valley Gate opened west or southwest from the old City of David toward the valley below; the Dung Gate stood about 1,000 cubits away at the south end (3:13), where the city's refuse was carried out. Where the Dragon Spring was is not known. The word for "dragon" means a serpent or great beast; a slightly different form means jackals.

decisions.choice: examining: looking closely, inspecting
decisions.reason: The verb is rare; in verse 15 it is used again of the wall. It means to look at something carefully in order to judge it.

decisions.choice: which were broken down: the written text and the reading tradition agree in sense
decisions.reason: The consonants of the text write a single word, "the ones broken down"; the Masoretic reading tradition reads two words, "they were broken down". The meaning is the same. This record follows the reading tradition, as the source data does.

decisions.choice: the Dragon Spring
decisions.reason: The first word means a spring rather than a dug well, so all levels say "spring"; the name keeps the word "dragon".

source.text: וָאֶֽעֱבֹר֙ אֶל־שַׁ֣עַר הָעַ֔יִן וְאֶל־בְּרֵכַ֖ת הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וְאֵין־מָק֥וֹם לַבְּהֵמָ֖ה לַעֲבֹ֥ר תַּחְתָּֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: And I passed on to [the] gate of the spring and to [the] pool of the king, and there was no place for the animal to pass under me.

en.L: And I passed on to the Fountain Gate and to the King's Pool, and there was no room for the animal under me to pass.
en.B: Then I went on to the Fountain Gate and to the King's Pool, but there was no room for the animal I was riding to get through.
en.R: Then I went on to the Fountain Gate and the King's Pool. But there was so much rubble that my animal could not get through.

decisions.choice: the Fountain Gate and the King's Pool: at the southeast of the city
decisions.reason: The Fountain Gate (literally "gate of the spring") was near the spring of Gihon or the pool fed by it. The King's Pool is probably the pool of Siloam, called in 3:15 "the Pool of Shelah by the king's garden" (compare 2 Kings 25:4).

decisions.choice: no room for the animal to pass: the way was blocked
decisions.reason: On the steep eastern slope the fallen stones of the wall, and of the terraces below it, blocked the path, so Nehemiah had to go down into the valley (verse 15).

decisions.choice: there was so much rubble
decisions.reason: Readable says why there was no room, which the broken walls of verse 13 make clear. The text itself says only that there was no room.

source.text: וָאֱהִ֨י עֹלֶ֤ה בַנַּ֨חַל֙ לַ֔יְלָה וָאֱהִ֥י שֹׂבֵ֖ר בַּחוֹמָ֑ה וָאָשׁ֗וּב וָאָב֛וֹא בְּשַׁ֥עַר הַגַּ֖יְא וָאָשֽׁוּב׃

records.literal_gloss: And I was going up in the valley [by] night, and I was examining the wall, and I turned back and came in by [the] gate of the valley, and returned.

en.L: And I was going up in the valley by night, and I was examining the wall. Then I turned back and came in through the Valley Gate, and so returned.
en.B: So I went up through the valley in the night and inspected the wall. Then I turned back and came in through the Valley Gate, and so I returned.
en.R: So I went up the Kidron Valley in the dark and looked closely at the wall. Then I turned around and went back in through the Valley Gate.

decisions.choice: the valley (wadi): the Kidron Valley, east of the city
decisions.reason: The word means a valley with a stream that runs in the rainy season. Going north from the King's Pool, below the eastern wall, this is the Kidron (2 Samuel 15:23; Jeremiah 31:40).

decisions.choice: I turned back ... and returned: he went back the way he came
decisions.reason: The verb "return" comes twice. Most likely he turned back in the Kidron and retraced his route to the Valley Gate, though he may have ridden on around the north of the city.

decisions.choice: the Kidron Valley
decisions.reason: Readable names the valley, which the route makes clear.

source.text: וְהַסְּגָנִ֗ים לֹ֤א יָדְעוּ֙ אָ֣נָה הָלַ֔כְתִּי וּמָ֖ה אֲנִ֣י עֹשֶׂ֑ה וְלַיְּהוּדִ֨ים וְלַכֹּהֲנִ֜ים וְלַחֹרִ֣ים וְלַסְּגָנִ֗ים וּלְיֶ֨תֶר֙ עֹשֵׂ֣ה הַמְּלָאכָ֔ה עַד־כֵּ֖ן לֹ֥א הִגַּֽדְתִּי׃

records.literal_gloss: And the officials not knew where I had gone and what I [was] doing; and to the Jews and to the priests and to the nobles and to the officials and to [the] rest of [the] doers of the work, until then not I had told.

en.L: And the officials did not know where I had gone or what I was doing. And to the Jews, the priests, the nobles, the officials and the rest who would do the work, I had not yet told anything.
en.B: The officials did not know where I had gone or what I was doing. I had not yet told the Jews, the priests, the nobles, the officials or the others who would do the work.
en.R: The city officials did not know where I had gone or what I was doing. I had not yet told anything to the Jews, the priests, the leaders, the officials or anyone else who would do the work.

decisions.choice: nobles and officials: the leading families and the appointed officers of Judah
decisions.reason: The first word names the free, leading men of the community; the second, officials with a set office, a word borrowed from Babylonian. The two appear together through the book (4:8; 5:7; 7:5).

decisions.choice: the doers of the work: those who would do the work
decisions.reason: The participle looks ahead: the work had not begun. "The work" is the rebuilding of the wall (4:5, 9).

decisions.choice: nobles (Literal, Balanced); leaders (Readable)
decisions.reason: The project's wording for this pair: Readable says "leaders" for nobles.

source.text: וָאוֹמַ֣ר אֲלֵהֶ֗ם אַתֶּ֤ם רֹאִים֙ הָרָעָה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר אֲנַ֣חְנוּ בָ֔הּ אֲשֶׁ֤ר יְרוּשָׁלִַ֨ם֙ חֲרֵבָ֔ה וּשְׁעָרֶ֖יהָ נִצְּת֣וּ בָאֵ֑שׁ לְכ֗וּ וְנִבְנֶה֙ אֶת־חוֹמַ֣ת יְרוּשָׁלִַ֔ם וְלֹא־נִהְיֶ֥ה ע֖וֹד חֶרְפָּֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And I said to them, you [are] seeing the trouble that we [are] in it, that Jerusalem [is] desolate and its gates have been burned with fire. Come and let us rebuild [the] wall of Jerusalem, and not we will be again a disgrace.

en.L: Then I said to them, "You see the trouble that we are in, that Jerusalem lies desolate and its gates have been burned with fire. Come, and let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, and we will no longer be a disgrace."
en.B: Then I said to them, "You see the trouble we are in: Jerusalem lies in ruins, and its gates have been burned with fire. Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, so that we will no longer be a disgrace."
en.R: Then I said to them, "You can see the trouble we are in. Jerusalem is in ruins, and its gates have been burned. Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem. Then people will no longer look down on us."

decisions.choice: a disgrace: an object of scorn to others
decisions.reason: This takes up the word of 1:3. Broken walls exposed the people to their neighbors' contempt and seemed to show that their God had abandoned them (Psalm 79:4; Lamentations 2:15-16).

decisions.choice: come and let us rebuild: an invitation, with Nehemiah one of the builders
decisions.reason: Nehemiah says "we" and "us": he counts himself among those in trouble and among those who will build.

decisions.choice: people will no longer look down on us
decisions.reason: Readable says what being a disgrace means, as in 1:3.

source.text: וָאַגִּ֨יד לָהֶ֜ם אֶת־יַ֣ד אֱלֹהַ֗י אֲשֶׁר־הִיא֙ טוֹבָ֣ה עָלַ֔י וְאַף־דִּבְרֵ֥י הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ אֲשֶׁ֣ר אָֽמַר־לִ֑י וַיֹּֽאמְרוּ֙ נָק֣וּם וּבָנִ֔ינוּ וַיְחַזְּק֥וּ יְדֵיהֶ֖ם לַטּוֹבָֽה׃פ

records.literal_gloss: And I told them [about] the hand of my God, that it [had been] good on me, and also [the] words of the king that he had spoken to me. And they said, let us arise and we will build! And they strengthened their hands for the good [work].

en.L: And I told them of the hand of my God, which had been good upon me, and also of the words of the king which he had spoken to me. And they said, "Let us arise and build!" And they strengthened their hands for the good work.
en.B: I told them how the hand of my God had been good to me, and also what the king had said to me. They said, "Let us start building!" So they prepared themselves for this good work.
en.R: I told them how kindly my God had helped me and what the king had said to me. They answered, "Let us start building now!" So they got ready and eagerly began this good work.

decisions.choice: the hand of my God that had been good on me: God's kind help
decisions.reason: As in verse 8: God's hand had been at work for Nehemiah, as the king's favor showed.

decisions.choice: they strengthened their hands for good: they took courage and set themselves to the work
decisions.reason: To strengthen the hands is to encourage, to give resolve for a task (Judges 7:11; Ezra 6:22). "For good" most likely means for the good work, the building; it may also mean "with good will".

decisions.choice: prepared themselves (Balanced); got ready and eagerly began (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the idiom "strengthened their hands" in plain words; Literal keeps it.

source.text: וַיִּשְׁמַע֩ סַנְבַלַּ֨ט הַחֹרֹנִ֜י וְטֹבִיָּ֣ה׀הָעֶ֣בֶד הָֽעַמּוֹנִ֗י וְגֶ֨שֶׁם֙ הָֽעַרְבִ֔י וַיַּלְעִ֣גוּ לָ֔נוּ וַיִּבְז֖וּ עָלֵ֑ינוּ וַיֹּאמְר֗וּ מָֽה־הַדָּבָ֤ר הַזֶּה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר אַתֶּ֣ם עֹשִׂ֔ים הַעַ֥ל הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ אַתֶּ֥ם מֹרְדִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: And heard Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite, and Geshem the Arab, and they mocked us and despised us and said, what [is] the thing, this, that you [are] doing? Against the king you [are] rebelling?

en.L: And when Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite, and Geshem the Arab heard, they mocked us and despised us and said, "What is this thing that you are doing? Are you rebelling against the king?"
en.B: But when Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite official and Geshem the Arab heard of it, they mocked us and scorned us. They said, "What is this you are doing? Are you rebelling against the king?"
en.R: But Sanballat from Horon, Tobiah the Ammonite official and Geshem the Arab heard about it. They laughed at us and insulted us. They said, "What do you think you are doing? Are you turning against the king?"

decisions.choice: Geshem the Arab: a ruler of Arab peoples to the south
decisions.reason: Geshem (6:1, 2, 6, where he is also called Gashmu) led Arab tribes in the lands south and east of Judah. An inscribed silver bowl from Egypt names a "Gashmu" as father of a king of Kedar, an Arab people of that time.

decisions.choice: are you rebelling against the king?: a charge of treason
decisions.reason: Building walls without the king's leave could be reported as preparing a revolt, the very charge that had stopped the work before (Ezra 4:12-16, 19-22). Nehemiah had the king's letters (verses 7-9), which the opponents ignore.

decisions.choice: official
decisions.reason: As in verse 10.

source.text: וָאָשִׁ֨יב אוֹתָ֜ם דָּבָ֗ר וָאוֹמַ֤ר לָהֶם֙ אֱלֹהֵ֣י הַשָּׁמַ֔יִם ה֚וּא יַצְלִ֣יחַֽ לָ֔נוּ וַאֲנַ֥חְנוּ עֲבָדָ֖יו נָק֣וּם וּבָנִ֑ינוּ וְלָכֶ֗ם אֵֽין־חֵ֧לֶק וּצְדָקָ֛ה וְזִכָּר֖וֹן בִּירוּשָׁלִָֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And I returned to them a word and said to them, [the] God of the heavens, he will make prosper us, and we, his slaves, will arise and we will build; and for you there is not a portion or a right or a memorial in Jerusalem.

en.L: And I answered them and said to them, "The God of heaven, he will make us prosper, and we {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} slaves will arise and build. But for you there is no portion or right or memorial in Jerusalem."
en.B: I answered them, "The God of heaven will give us success, and we {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} servants will start building. But you have no share, no right and no memorial in Jerusalem."
en.R: I answered them, "The God of heaven will help us succeed, and we are {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} servants. We will start building. But you have no part in Jerusalem. You have no right to it, and you will not be remembered here."

decisions.choice: the God of heaven, he will make us prosper: our success depends on God, not on the king or on you
decisions.reason: The pronoun "he" is written out for emphasis. Nehemiah answers the charge of rebellion by naming the higher authority he serves.

decisions.choice: no portion, no right, no memorial in Jerusalem: no place in its community at all
decisions.reason: A portion is a share as by inheritance; a right is a legal claim; a memorial is a lasting remembrance there, such as a name kept in its records or worship. Together the three words shut the opponents out of Jerusalem's life and affairs.

decisions.choice: his slaves: those who belong to God and serve him
decisions.reason: As in 1:6. Nehemiah's "we" here is the people of Jerusalem who build.

decisions.choice: slaves (Literal); servants (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 1:6, the project's rule for this word.
